newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FOCUS - C.Lyonnais to sell Woodchester stake.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - C.Lyonnais to sell Woodchester stake.

text.p: Woodchester Investments Plc announced on Thursday that Credit Lyonnais will sell its 54 percent stake in the group. The move is expected to lead to a full bid for the Irish financial services group.
Woodchester is valued at 600 million Irish pounds ($935.6 million) and its takeover will be the largest in the history of the Irish stock exchange.

Troubled Credit Lyonnais, which has been under pressure to divest of holdings outside France to win EU approval for a second financial rescue package, sees the Irish company as a valuable asset and said it will seek a price which reflects the full value of its shareholding.
Chairman Craig McKinney said Woodchester was in excellent shape and ready to face the challenges of the tasks ahead.
"I look forward to the future with confidence," McKinney said in a results statement.
A spokesman for Woodchester said Craig McKinney was not available for comment after the announcement.
Woodchester reported an increase of 22 percent in 1996 pre-tax profit to 44 million pounds ($68.6 million) on Thursday and said new business was up 30 percent in the first two months of 1997.

"Last year all business units achieved considerable growth," Woodchester said. "This has continued into 1997, with new business for the first two months up by over 30 percent on the corresponding period last year."
Analysts expect potential buyers will have to pay a premium on Woodchester's current share price of 279 Irish pence, up from 218 pence at the start of the year.

GE Capital is tipped as the front runner in the race to acquire the Irish group. Other names mentioned include National Westminster Banks' Irish unit Ulster Bank, which owns Lombard and Ulster leasing operation and Chartered Trust, owned by Standard Chartered.

A buyer of the Credit Lyonnais stake would be required under Stock Exchange rules to make a similar offer to the remaining shareholders. But such a buyer could seek a dispensation from Stock Exchange requirements if the other shareholders agreed. Credit Lyonnais got a dispensation when it raised its stake in Woodchester above the 50 percent level.

Woodchester's chairman McKinney, would be a beneficiary of any sale. At the end of 1995 he owned 2.56 million shares which are now worth more than seven million Irish pounds. In addition, he has options over an additional 759,986 shares at an average option price of 157.74p.
